title: ITD 256 Midterm Study Guide
description: Comprehensive notes covering everything the midterm quiz tests, organized to match the exam's three parts: Theory & SQL, ERD Completion, and Normalization & Dependency Sets.

blocks.text: File & Database Terminology

rows: Raw facts (e.g. a phone number, birth date) with little meaning until organized.
A character or group of characters with specific meaning, used to define and store data. Also called an **attribute**.
A logically connected set of fields describing a person, place, or thing. Also called an **entity instance**.
A collection of related records. Called a **Table** (or entity) once you're inside a DBMS.

blocks.label: Build order:
blocks.text: Data → Field → Record → Table. Each level is built out of the one before it.
Types of Databases

items: **By structure:** Unstructured (raw, no formatting) → Semistructured (partially processed, e.g. XML) → Structured (fully formatted/processed).
**By location:** Centralized (single site) · Distributed (spread across sites) · Cloud (maintained via a cloud service with defined performance measures).

**By use:** Analytical / data warehouse databases store historical data for decision support. **OLAP** = tools to retrieve/process/model data from a warehouse. **Business intelligence** = capturing and processing business data to support decisions.

blocks.text: Structural & Data (In)dependence

rows: File access depends on its own structure — changing the structure breaks every program that reads it.
The file structure can change without breaking the programs that access it.
How data is accessed changes whenever the storage characteristics change.
Storage characteristics can change without affecting the program's ability to access the data.

blocks.text: **Logical format** = how data is represented to the application/user. **Physical format** = how it's actually stored on hardware. The physical format should be completely hidden from the user — that's the whole point of data independence.
Data Redundancy & Anomalies
**Data redundancy**: unnecessarily storing the same data in different places, which raises the risk of ending up with different (inconsistent) versions of that data.

items: **Update anomaly** — a change made in one place isn't propagated everywhere, leaving inconsistent/incomplete data.
**Insertion anomaly** — you can't insert a new record without also supplying data you don't have yet.
**Deletion anomaly** — deleting one record accidentally destroys other data you still needed.

blocks.text: DBMS Functions

rows: Stores definitions of data elements and their relationships.
Handles efficient storage and performance tuning.
Formats data to match the user's logical expectations.
Enforces user security and data privacy.
Lets many users access the database concurrently without compromising integrity.
Enables recovery of the database after a failure.
The de facto standard for accessing data across nearly every DBMS vendor.

blocks.text: Data Model Building Blocks

items: **Entity** — a person, place, thing, or event.
**Attribute** — a characteristic of an entity.
**Relationship** — an association among entities (1:1, 1:M, or M:N).
**Constraint** — a restriction placed on data to ensure data integrity.

blocks.text: When translating business rules into a model: **nouns** become entities, **verbs** become relationships. Relationships are always **bidirectional** — always ask the cardinality question from both entities' points of view.

blocks.label: Notation:
blocks.text: Chen notation (diamonds for relationships) is the most **abstract** / conceptual style. Crow's Foot notation (used in this course) is less abstract. DDL SQL is the least abstract — it's the actual implementation.
The Relational Model & Keys

A **relation** = a **table** = an **entity**: a matrix of intersecting rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). An **RDBMS** makes this model easy to use by hiding its underlying complexity from the user.

rows: The attribute or combination of attributes that uniquely identifies a row.
A real-world identifier already familiar to end users (e.g. a SSN or ISBN) that can double as a primary key.
An artificial, made-up key (e.g. an auto-number). Useful when there's no good natural key, or the PK would otherwise be composite/too long.
A key made up of more than one attribute.
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row — may include unnecessary attributes.
Used strictly for data retrieval (e.g. searching by last name), not for uniqueness.
A copy of one table's primary key, placed in another table to link the two.

blocks.text: Integrity Rules

rows: All primary key values are unique, and no part of the primary key can be null.
Every foreign key value must be either **null**, or match an existing primary key value in the related table.

blocks.label: Tip:
blocks.text: "NULL" means the absence of a data value (unknown, missing, or not applicable) — it is not the same as zero or an empty string.
Data Dictionary, System Catalog, and Schema

items: **Data dictionary** — description of all tables, created by the user/designer.
**System catalog** — the DBMS's own automatically-maintained data dictionary.
**Database schema** — the complete logical view of the entire database.
**Relational schema** — the same idea, but scoped to one individual table.

blocks.text: Relationship Types

items: **1:M** — the norm for relational databases; the most common relationship type.
**1:1** — one entity instance relates to at most one instance of the other entity.

**M:N** — valid at the conceptual (ERD) level, but can't be implemented directly in a relational table. It requires a **bridge / composite / associative entity** holding both related primary keys as foreign keys.

blocks.label: Golden rule:
blocks.text: The foreign key always goes on the "many" side of a 1:M relationship, referencing the primary key on the "one" side.
SQL Command Categories

rows: Data Definition Language — defines the database structure
Data Manipulation Language — manipulates the data itself
Data Control Language — controls access permissions
Permanently delete an entire database, including all tables.
Create a new table — can include NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, DEFAULT, and CHECK constraints.
Modify an existing table's definition (add/modify/delete attributes or constraints).
Permanently delete a table and its data.
Create or delete an index on a table.
Create or delete a dynamic subset of rows/columns from one or more tables.

blocks.text: SELECT Statement Anatomy

SELECT   columnlist
FROM     tablelist
[WHERE   conditionlist]
[GROUP BY columnlist]
[HAVING  conditionlist]
[ORDER BY columnlist [ASC | DESC]];

rows: Specifies the table(s) data is retrieved from.
Filters individual **rows** based on given criteria.
Groups rows into collections that share the same value(s).
Filters the **groups** formed by GROUP BY (not individual rows).
Sorts the final result rows, ascending or descending.

blocks.label: Build order:
blocks.text: Write a query one clause at a time, always in this order — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, [GROUP BY], [HAVING], ORDER BY.
Joins Reference

items: **Inner join** — returns only rows that match in both tables.
**Outer join** (left / right / full) — returns matched rows, plus unmatched rows from one or both sides.
**NATURAL JOIN** — auto-matches identically-named, compatible-type columns and eliminates duplicate columns. No ON/USING needed.
**JOIN ... USING (column)** — matches on a named column that must exist (with the same name) in both tables.
**JOIN ... ON (condition)** — an explicit join condition; required when the tables have no identically-named common column.
**Recursive / self / unary join** — a table joined to itself (e.g. matching an employee to their own manager). All other joins are binary (between two different tables).
Old-style joins (`WHERE table1.pk = table2.fk`) still work, but aren't recommended — harder to maintain and easier to get wrong.

blocks.text: WHERE Clause Operators

items: **AND / OR / NOT** — combine multiple conditions.
**BETWEEN ... AND ...** — tests a range, inclusive of both endpoints.
**IN** — tests whether a value matches any value in a given list.
**LIKE** — pattern matching; `%` matches any sequence of zero or more characters, `_` matches exactly one character.
**IS NULL / IS NOT NULL** — tests whether a value is missing.

blocks.text: Aggregate Functions

rows: The number of rows (or non-null values) in a set.
The smallest / largest value in a set.
The total of all values in a set.
The mean (average) of all values in a set.

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: Aggregate functions reduce a whole collection of rows down to a single summary row.
Data Manipulation (DML) Syntax

blocks.label: Careful:
blocks.text: SQL does NOT ask for confirmation. An UPDATE or DELETE run without a WHERE clause immediately applies to every row in the table. Always use WHERE to limit the damage.
**CRUD** = Create, Read, Update, Delete → maps to (C) **INSERT**, (R) **SELECT**, (U) **UPDATE**, (D) **DELETE**.
The "Connector Options" Legend

This professor's exam ERDs use a 6-letter legend of Crow's Foot symbols to mark cardinality and participation on each end of a relationship line. Two of the six (A and D) are deliberate distractors — incomplete symbols that don't actually specify a valid combination.

rows: Not valid alone — a crow's foot needs a participation mark too.
One or many (**mandatory many** — "at least one").
Not valid alone — a bar alone doesn't say one-or-many.

blocks.text:
Mandatory one   (E):  ────||
Optional one    (F):  ────O|
Mandatory many  (B):  ────|<
Optional many   (C):  ────O<

blocks.label: The pattern:
blocks.text: Cardinality (one vs. many) = a single line vs. a crow's foot. Participation (mandatory vs. optional) = a double bar vs. a circle. A valid connector always combines exactly one of each.
How to Read a Business Rule Into Cardinality & Participation

items: Identify the two entities in the relationship, and read the business rule from each entity's point of view, one direction at a time.
Ask: "What's the **maximum** number of [Entity B] related to one [Entity A]?" → gives you the **cardinality** (one, or many).
Ask: "Is [Entity A] **required** to have at least one related [Entity B]?" → gives you the **participation** (mandatory, or optional).
Repeat from the other entity's point of view — remember, relationships are always bidirectional, so each end gets its own connector.

blocks.text: Worked example
"A DEPARTMENT must employ at least one EMPLOYEE, and can employ many. Every EMPLOYEE must work for exactly one DEPARTMENT."

items: DEPARTMENT end (viewed from EMPLOYEE's side): mandatory, max **one** → connector **E**.
EMPLOYEE end (viewed from DEPARTMENT's side): mandatory, max **many** → connector **B**.

blocks.text: Reading Entity Boxes: PK / FK / Descriptive Attributes

rows: **Bold + underlined**, listed first, above the dividing line
Descriptive (non-key / regular) attribute — describes the entity, but doesn't identify rows or link tables

blocks.text: Relationship Types & How They're Implemented

items: **1:M** (most common) — the foreign key goes on the "many" side, referencing the primary key on the "one" side.
**1:1** — one entity relates to at most one other; place the FK on whichever side makes structural sense (often the optional/dependent side).

**M:N** — can't be implemented directly in a relational table. Requires a **bridge (composite/associative) entity**. That bridge entity's primary key is typically the **composite** of both parent primary keys, each also stored as a foreign key.
Once a bridge entity exists, the single M:N relationship becomes **two 1:M relationships** — the bridge entity sits on the "many" side of each.

blocks.text: Normal Forms Summary

rows: Table format, no repeating groups, and the primary key identified.

blocks.label: Shortcut:
blocks.text: If a 1NF table's primary key is a single attribute (not composite), it automatically satisfies 2NF too — partial dependencies can only exist against part of a composite key.
Key Vocabulary

items: **Functional dependence** — A determines B (written `A -> B`) if every value of A corresponds to exactly one value of B. A is the **determinant**, B is the **dependent** attribute.
**Full functional dependence** — B depends on the *entire* composite key A, not on any subset of it.
**Partial dependency** — an attribute depends on only *part* of a composite primary key. Only possible when the PK is composite — usually straightforward to spot.

**Transitive dependency** — a non-key attribute depends on *another non-key attribute*, rather than directly on the primary key. Trickier to spot, since it only happens between two non-key (nonprime) attributes.
**Repeating group** — multiple entries of the same type of data repeated for one key occurrence (e.g. COURSE_ID_1, COURSE_ID_2, COURSE_ID_3). The first thing removed on the way to 1NF.

blocks.text: The Normalization Procedure

items: **Convert to 1NF:** eliminate repeating groups → identify the primary key → identify all dependencies (a dependency diagram helps make sure none are overlooked).
**Convert to 2NF:** remove partial dependencies — move each partially-dependent attribute into its own new table, keyed on whatever determines it.
**Convert to 3NF:** remove transitive dependencies — move the chained attribute(s) into their own new table, keyed on the non-key attribute that determines them.

blocks.text: Worked Example: ASSIGNMENT table
1NF table: **ASSIGNMENT**(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM, PROJ_NAME, EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR, HOURS) — composite PK (PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM).

Dependency set:
PROJ_NUM -> PROJ_NAME                          (partial)
EMP_NUM  -> EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR      (partial)
(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM) -> HOURS                   (full, on composite key)

2NF decomposition (partial dependencies removed):
PROJECT(PROJ_NUM, PROJ_NAME)
EMPLOYEE(EMP_NUM, EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR)
ASSIGNMENT(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM, HOURS)
But inside EMPLOYEE, EMP_NUM determines JOB_CLASS, and JOB_CLASS determines CHG_HOUR — so EMP_NUM -> CHG_HOUR is a **transitive dependency**.

3NF decomposition (transitive dependency removed):
EMPLOYEE(EMP_NUM, EMP_NAME, JOB_CLASS)
JOB(JOB_CLASS, CHG_HOUR)
PROJECT(PROJ_NUM, PROJ_NAME)
ASSIGNMENT(PROJ_NUM, EMP_NUM, HOURS)
Denormalization
Denormalization deliberately produces a **lower** normal form. It trades increased redundancy for fewer joins and faster reads.

items: **Redundant data** — e.g. storing both ZIP and CITY when ZIP determines CITY, to avoid an extra join.
**Derived / preaggregated data** — e.g. storing a precomputed STU_GPA instead of recalculating it from ENROLL/COURSE every time.
**Reporting requirements** — a temporary denormalized table built just to produce a tabular report.

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: More tables (from normalizing) generally means more join operations to reconstruct the full picture — that's the core tradeoff normalization makes.
